title: ASIC warns scammers are using AI to spin vast webs of deception

reading.body:
AI-generated impersonation has been deployed at scale in investment fraud. Scammers created fake news articles featuring real public figures like a Reserve Bank governor and finance presenter, paired with fabricated endorsements of unlicensed cryptocurrency platforms. The system worked because the false content circulated online before removal, and because it exploited the difficulty of distinguishing AI-generated text and deepfakes from authentic reporting.

The failure occurred in the open internet ecosystem where content moderation happens after publication rather than before. No human verification of the article's authenticity or the endorsement's legitimacy stood between creation and distribution. Catching this would have required either the hosting platforms to authenticate articles before hosting them, or readers to verify the sources independently, or the financial platform itself to be blocked before scammers could reference it.

It is not established whether the AI systems were purpose-built for fraud or repurposed from legitimate generative tools. The incident shows scammers using AI as a capability to scale impersonation and fabrication rather than a failure of AI systems themselves to behave as intended.

reports.title: The fake Alan Kohler interview that shows a type of scam that’s on the rise
AI deepfake scams 'an emergency in the making' as ASIC reports rise in false investment endorsements
ASIC warns scammers are using AI to spin vast webs of deception

summary:
# Summary

A fake online article featuring Reserve Bank governor Michele Bullock in a heated interview with ABC finance presenter Alan Kohler was recently removed from the internet. The fabricated piece promoted Boulder Sparhaven, an unlicensed cryptocurrency trading platform that Australian authorities warn against. This incident exemplifies a growing category of investment scams that use artificial intelligence to create convincing deepfakes and false content featuring prominent Australians. ASIC reports that such schemes are becoming increasingly sophisticated and widespread.

Research released by the Australian Securities and Investments Commission shows that AI-generated investment scams are rising significantly. Last year, ASIC removed 19,400 scams, a 182 percent increase, including 7,051 fake investment platforms and 5,476 phishing scams. Prime Minister Anthony Albanese, along with politicians, financial experts, businesspeople, and wealthy individuals like Gina Rinehart, are commonly impersonated. Scammers build elaborate networks of fake websites, news articles, and advertisements to deceive consumers. ASIC advises people to verify Australian Financial Services licence numbers and independently check company legitimacy before investing.
